chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far (the second Imam), peace be upon him: 'I am your ransom, indeed a man from our companions threw the Jamarah on the day of Nahr (sacrifice) and shaved [his head] before he slaughtered [the animal].' He said: 'Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was visited on the day of Nahr by groups of Muslims who said: O Messenger of Allah, we slaughtered before we threw [the Jamarah] and we shaved before we slaughtered, so nothing that ought to be done first was left except that it was delayed, and nothing that ought to be done last was left except that it was done first.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'No harm, no harm.' Therefore, the interpretation of this report is that we should understand it as applying to one who did that out of forgetfulness or unintentionally, and indeed doing that is not permissible on the path of deliberate intent.

key_terms.يَوْمَ النَّحْرِ: Day of Sacrifice (10th of Dhu al-Hijjah)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a pilgrim shaves before slaughtering during Hajj?
ai.summary: In *Al-Istibsar*, Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration to clarify the sequence of Hajj rites, specifically prohibiting shaving before slaughter. The hadith highlights the Prophetic precedent of leniency (*la haraj*) for the Companions who acted out of order, which Shia jurists interpret as applying to unintentional or forgetful actions, while deliberate deviation remains invalid.
